Documentation → Releases → 1.11.0

SATOM 1.11.0

Introduces Sentinel for security incident correlation and controlled response, external vault storage for credentials, the WAF Artifacts store, and ADOM-aware handling of physical appliances.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-08-20 · All releases

In short#

A large release with four big themes. Sentinel is a new security module that groups attack events, traffic outcomes, appliance and infrastructure metrics and vulnerability data into scored incidents, and can carry out a small, tightly controlled set of responses. Credentials can now be kept in an external vault instead of in SATOM itself. A new WAF Artifacts store lets clones and migrations copy file-based WAF objects (schemas, API definitions, Lua scripts) with their content, not just their name. And SATOM now understands that several ADOM rows can be one physical appliance, which changes the appliance list, capacity figures and clone checks. Security teams, operators who clone policies and administrators will all see changes.

What's new#

Sentinel — security correlation#

Sentinel is a new module that correlates FortiWeb attack signatures, HTTP response outcomes, appliance counters, virtual machine and hypervisor metrics and vulnerability intelligence into incidents. Each incident explains itself from the evidence it was built on.

  • Pages: a console, an incident page, a Context page, a documentation page and a response-policy page, plus a Sentinel section in Settings.
  • Background work: three scheduled actions — the sweep, the baseline calculation and the vulnerability data sync. A fresh installation sets them up automatically, and the installation diagnosis reports a missing sweep. Without the sweep Sentinel opens no incidents and looks exactly like a quiet week.

How Sentinel decides, in plain terms:

  • The AI assistant does not decide. It reads a finished incident and writes a narrative and a recommendation. It has no tools, no credentials and cannot change a score. If every AI component is down, Sentinel still detects, scores, explains and gates — it only loses the narrative.
  • "Normal" is learned per hour of the week, in a way that an attack in the training data cannot drag upwards. A new or flat data series never raises an alarm on its own.
  • Some evidence lowers the score. A wall of attacks the appliance already blocked does not page anyone; an exploit aimed at software the backend does not run is treated as noise; and an authorised scanner is recognised by its context.
  • A layer that was not measured shows "unknown", never "no impact". These lead to opposite decisions, so they are never mixed up.
  • Vulnerability data stays on the node. Incidents are enriched from a local copy, never by asking an outside service, so no third party gets a live map of what is being attacked. Downloading that local copy is a separate switch, off by default. Exploitation likelihood and known-exploited status outrank the plain severity score.

Sentinel — responses#

Sentinel can propose responses and, for verified actions, carry them out. Every proposal passes through thirteen gates, checked in a fixed order.

  • Block an IP address is the first action that can actually run. It was tested end to end on a live FortiWeb. A separate runner, which checks once a minute, re-checks every gate at the moment it acts and asks the appliance whether it can enforce the block before writing.
  • A block is only marked applied after SATOM reads it back from the appliance. Whether it actually helped is judged separately: an action that landed but changed nothing returns its incident from mitigated and is never retried.
  • Blocks expire. Expiry runs even when the kill switch is off, so disarming cannot leave a block in place, and the appliance also carries its own block period so it lifts the block even if Sentinel is down.
  • Block a country and raise protection (move a policy to a stronger profile) were also tested on a live appliance. A country is stored exactly as the appliance reports it — a full country name; a short country code is refused with a reason rather than guessed. Raising protection has no timer on the appliance, so SATOM reads and keeps the previous profile first, and refuses an undo that would leave the policy with no profile at all.
  • Tune a signature writes nothing to an appliance; it drafts an exception that a person applies in the existing exception workflow. The console now says so plainly instead of reporting "level too low".
  • Autonomy (level 3) lets a policy skip the approval step for a decision the gates already allowed. It ships disarmed. It can never raise a limit, widen an action or extend a block, and blocking a country always stays at recommend. A decision stays one proposal per incident and action, however many sweeps see it.
  • On the Context page you can now arm responses: binding Sentinel's IP list to a policy's protection profile is an explicit human action recorded in the audit log. Country blocking is armed separately from address blocking, so the larger decision is never a side effect of the smaller one.
  • A new setting lists the hardened profiles that "raise protection" may move a policy onto. It is empty by default, which means that action cannot run until an administrator chooses the profiles.
  • The Sentinel documentation page shows four diagrams — the reference architecture, the processing pipeline, the decision ladder and the response / verification / rollback loop. They need no JavaScript, so they also work in an offline bundle and in print.

New collectors: HTTP status and infrastructure#

Two new collectors appear on the same page as every other collector, where you set their cadence:

  • HTTP status counts response classes from the traffic log.
  • Infrastructure collects virtual machine and hypervisor node metrics. This is available for Proxmox; a hypervisor that cannot answer is reported as unknown, not as healthy. Counters survive a VM restart.

Credentials in an external vault (Settings → Vault)#

A new Settings → Vault tab lets you keep appliance passwords, the LDAP/AD bind password and the FortiAuthenticator shared secret in an OpenBao or HashiCorp Vault store. Keeping them in SATOM remains the default: if you never open this tab, nothing changes and nothing is contacted.

The reason to use it: SATOM's own encryption key sits on the same server as the database it protects, so anyone who can read that disk can read every appliance password. A vault moves the secrets off the node. There are three modes, and the page explains what each costs:

  • Local — SATOM only (the default).
  • Mirror — both. SATOM reads from the vault first and falls back to its own copy. Safe to roll back from, but the local copy still exists, so the exposure is not yet closed.
  • Vault — the vault is the only copy. This closes the exposure, and it also means a vault outage makes credentials unavailable.

Moving secrets into the vault is a dry run by default, and each secret is read back before it counts as moved.

A Remove the local copies card on the same tab completes the move. Until it runs, switching to vault only changes where the next write goes: credentials already stored keep their local copy. Removing is deliberately a separate step, because copying can be undone and removing cannot:

  • it is refused unless the vault is the authoritative store;
  • it is a dry run by default;
  • every secret is read back from the vault and compared with the local copy first; if the vault copy is missing, different or unreachable, the local copy is kept and the row is reported as failed.

WAF Artifacts#

Seven kinds of API-protection objects — XML Schema, XML DTD, WSDL, OpenAPI, gRPC IDL, JSON Schema and Lua scripts — keep only their name in the appliance configuration. A clone used to create them empty at the destination: a rule bound to an empty object was refused, or, worse, if the rule already existed the policy silently ran with that protection off.

The new WAF Artifacts page keeps the file content in SATOM. It is included in standby replication and system backups. Three actions:

  • Upload — hand SATOM the file. This is the only way XML Schema, WSDL and gRPC IDL can ever be stored, because no FortiWeb gives them back.
  • Capture — read the content live from a device (for the four types that can be read).
  • Push — write a stored copy onto an appliance.

Clone and migrate now copy the content too. Every file-based object in a plan is resolved before the first write — from the source device first, then from SATOM's store — and uploaded to the destination with its content.

When no content can be found, the pre-flight checklist shows a warning naming the object and the consequence, and Apply stays disabled until you tick clone anyway. The warning stays a warning after you accept it, because the destination is still incomplete.

Interface roles and the interface check in clones#

  • When you register an appliance — now including the Add Appliance dialog, which previously collected no interfaces — you can give each port a role (management, front-side traffic, back-side traffic, one-arm, inline pair, HA sync, HA reserved, mirror, unused, other) and a segment (free text, such as "DMZ / VLAN 20"). Both are also editable on the appliance edit page. Existing ports show Not declared, because the device itself cannot tell what a port is for. Rediscovery never overwrites them.
  • Clone and migrate check which port the copy will use. A new pre-flight row checks every interface the copied objects refer to against the destination's ports, and a selector lets you map each source port to a destination port:
  • port missing at the destination → blocked;
  • port exists but neither side declared its role → warning;
  • roles or segments disagree → warning naming both.

Your mapping is applied to the objects that are created.

One physical appliance, several ADOM rows#

A FortiWeb in ADOM mode has to be registered once per ADOM, so one box appeared in SATOM as several devices. SATOM now recognises rows that share the same device address as one chassis:

  • The appliance list folds the ADOMs under their device. Firmware, the CLI console and the configuration-backup vault act on the whole box, so they are offered — and enforced — only on the row for the root ADOM. (Restoring a backup from another ADOM's row would in fact have restored every ADOM.) Classification, policies, discovery and each row's own credential stay per ADOM. The fold remembers what you opened, and search still finds rows inside it.
  • The header tiles count appliances, not rows, so the Online and Offline totals add up. HA cluster members still count separately, because they are separate boxes. A new fifth tile shows how many ADOMs those appliances carry.
  • Capacity headroom counts the whole chassis, instead of giving each ADOM row its own budget against one shared CPU, and the message says so.
  • Interface roles are shared across the chassis, with a row's own declaration winning over a sibling's.
  • Clone and migrate warn when source and destination are the same box. Moving a policy between two ADOMs of one chassis does not move it off that hardware.

A device registered only once is unaffected.

Server Objects matches the FortiWeb menu again#

The Server Objects menu had drifted from the appliance. It now follows the FortiWeb menu — entries, order and the tabs inside pages:

  • Certificates has twelve entries. XML Certificate, URL Certificate, Sign CA, Certificate Verify and Public Key Pinning were missing; CA Group, TSL CA and Intermediate CA Group are now tabs inside another page, as on the appliance; Multi-certificate and Offline SNI were added as tabs.
  • Traffic Mirror, Global Allow List, Policy Based Allow List and URL Replacer were added elsewhere in the section.
  • Object lists now show a tab strip where FortiWeb groups several lists on one page.

What changes for you#

  • Virtual IP moved to the Network menu, where FortiWeb files it.
  • A file-based object with no content is skipped, not created empty. It is marked no content in the plan and in the clone report, and a rule that needs it then fails visibly instead of looking configured.
  • A migration no longer disables the source if anything was skipped. Accepting a missing artifact allows an incomplete copy, not an unprotected cut-over.
  • Sentinel's "rate limit IP" action was removed. FortiWeb's flood-prevention rules apply to every client of a profile, not to a single address, so the action could not deliver what it promised. Policy rows that only referred to it are cleaned up.
  • The response runner only runs on the primary node. A standby — or a node that cannot tell what it is — refuses to apply or expire blocks, so two nodes can never fight over the same appliance.

Fixed#

  • Policies with Lua scripts could not be cloned. Any policy with one or more scripts was refused with "source tree incomplete", even when the script already existed on the destination. Scripts are now read correctly, also in configuration snapshots (which had been leaving the script out) and when their content is copied (which would otherwise have created an empty script).
  • The Intermediate CA page never worked on any firmware, because it pointed at a list that does not exist. It now shows the right list, and the broken entry no longer appears in the general Configuration browser.
  • A US source showed as "United S". Country names in Sentinel were cut to 8 characters, which also made them unusable for country blocking. They now hold the full name, and existing records are widened automatically.
  • System health did not mention the response runner. A node where it is off can hold a block nobody will ever lift; the health output now reports it.
  • Running Sentinel's command-line tool from a plain shell reported a clean pass against an empty development database while a real block sat on a firewall. It now refuses and tells you which service to use instead.
  • An XML DTD that could be read was reported as unreadable, because of a stray byte the firmware adds. It now reads correctly.
  • OpenAPI files came back with every line break doubled, which for YAML changes the document. Fixed.
  • An ADOM-mode device with no ADOM selected showed an empty policy list and no error. The affected row was set to the root ADOM. There is not yet an automatic guard against this — check that each row of an ADOM-mode device has an ADOM.
  • The user guide's page and exclusion counts for the Concept Map were corrected.

Before you upgrade#

  • After changing the credential storage mode, restart every SATOM process, not only the main web service. A background process still running the old code sent the vault placeholder to every appliance as a password: every collector failed to log in and nothing in the vault's log explained why. Both read paths now refuse instead, but a restart of all processes is still required.
  • VLAN interfaces must be created over the CLI. FortiWeb 7.6.8 does not offer VLANs through its web API, and SATOM currently shows that as an empty list rather than an error.
  • Raise protection stays off until you list hardened profiles in the Sentinel settings.

Under the hood#

  • The local repository configuration file, which holds the push token for the Git server, is now readable only by its owner — on existing installations and on every new one.
  • Sentinel's response runner timer is installed and enabled by the installer, so a new node can lift expired blocks.
  • The engineering manual now documents how a change is promoted from the standby through the primary to the code server, and how SATOM is tested.
